definition: Stating opinions as if they are certainly true and refusing to consider other views.
example: A dogmatic coach may ignore new training research simply because it contradicts his favorite drills.
nuance: A confident person holds views firmly; a dogmatic person also refuses to examine them or hear any challenge.
prompt: A science teacher responds to a student who questions a claim in the textbook.
options: The dogmatic teacher waved away the student's evidence and simply repeated the textbook's claim.
The dogmatic teacher happily revised the lesson after reviewing the student's data.
The dogmatic teacher kept grading lab reports late into the night until all were done.
The dogmatic teacher flung both arms wide and gasped theatrically at the question.
reasons: Dismissing evidence without examining it shows rigid, unquestioning certainty.
Welcoming new evidence and changing one's view is the opposite of this rigidity.
Tireless persistence describes being dogged, a look-alike, not refusing other views.
A showy, theatrical reaction confuses the word with dramatic.

practice.prompt: Members of a hiking club disagree about which trail to take up the mountain.
options: Ravi was so dogmatic that he chose whichever trail suited the morning's weather report.
Ravi was so dogmatic that he brought his two beagles along on every club hike.
Ravi was so dogmatic about his route that he dismissed the new map before even opening it.
Ravi was so dogmatic that he asked everyone for ideas and adopted the most popular route.
reasons: Adapting to current conditions is practical flexibility, closer to pragmatic.
The word comes from dogma, meaning fixed belief, and has nothing to do with dogs.
Rejecting information unseen shows a belief held beyond question.
Inviting input and changing course shows open-mindedness, not rigidity.
